tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

task_id.description: The task_id returned by the spawn_task call that created the chip.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the currently attached simulator, or the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

#!/bin/sh
# Block secrets and .env files, run ruff if Python is set up. Enable once: git config core.hooksPath .githooks
pattern='(OPENAI_API_KEY|ANTHROPIC_API_KEY|[A-Z_]*_API_KEY)[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*["'"'"']?[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}|sk-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,}'
if git diff --cached --name-only | grep -v '\.env\.example$' | grep -Eq '(^|/)\.env(\..*)?$'; then
  echo "Blocked: .env file staged." >&2; exit 1
fi
hits=$(git diff --cached -U0 | grep '^+' | grep -v '^+++' | grep -E "$pattern" | head -5)
if [ -n "$hits" ]; then
  echo "Blocked: possible secret in commit. Move it to .env (gitignored)." >&2
  echo "$hits" >&2; exit 1

# Negotiation Arena: Agent Policies & Orchestration

Oct 10, 2026 · @Julian

## Principles

Code owns every number and every binding decision; the LLM reads people and writes e-mails. Score is total cost C, so the agent optimises C, never price alone.

| Decision | Owner | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Term sheets (all fields) | Code: optimiser over `term_options` + `total_cost` | Only term sheets bind; arithmetic in an LLM leaks money |
| Accept / walk away | Code: closing gate | A broken must-have scores 0; a deal worse than the alternative is a loss |
| Which claims to cite | Code picks from a pre-verified claim bank; LLM may rank | `contradicted` costs trust; only 3 claims are checked per message |
| Strategy per supplier (archetype, levers) | LLM offline (dossier), code applies it live | Heavy reading must not eat the 60 s clock |
| Reading a reply (signals, cost drivers named, cash interest, approval hints) | LLM, structured JSON | Suppliers explain themselves in prose |
| E-mail wording and tone | LLM, small fast model | Suppliers react to tone; padding buys nothing |

Three rules hold everywhere:

1. Never send what code has not checked: every term sheet completed and snapped, every ID in `facts.json` or the case's `facts`, every figure recomputed.
2. Never leak urgency, budget, target price or a missing alternative.
3. Every move must be reciprocal: no concession without a move from the supplier, never two concessions in a row.

## Architecture

[embedded content: agent architecture · offline layer, wave runner, coordinator, thread negotiators\]

Dossiers are built once before the final. During a wave, each supplier thread loops reader → policy engine → writer → guard, and only the policy engine sets terms. The case coordinator owns the plan, the shared blackboard and the decision to close.

## Orchestration and timing

The kit's `play()` sends one message at a time across all threads of a case, so a 3-supplier RFQ gets only 2-3 rounds per supplier inside a wave. Replace it with one negotiator per thread running in parallel under a case coordinator; keep the kit's `play_waves()` polling and resume logic.

| Budget item | Value | Source / assumption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wave cap | 480 s (read `seconds_left`, never assume) | Brief |
| Forced close before cap | max(90 s, slowest round + 15 s) | Kit `CLOSE_BEFORE_CAP_S` |
| Usable negotiation time | about 390 s | 480 − 90 |
| Supplier reply | up to about 60 s, does not count against us | API docs |
| Our decision per move | target 15 s, LLM hard timeout 35 s, template fallback at 45 s | 60 s rule; 3 timeouts in a row end the thread |
| Rounds per thread (parallel) | about 5-7 | 390 s / (15 s + 40-60 s) |
| Rounds per thread (kit, 3-supplier RFQ) | about 2-3 | Same time split three ways |
| Concurrency | 10 open sessions, 10 calls/s per key | API docs |

Consequences for every policy below:

- Plan for 4 substantive rounds, not 10. Round 1 must already carry the anchor and the probe sheets.
- Case-open work (read case, load dossier, plan) must finish in 20 s: the 60 s clock starts when the session opens. Everything heavy is precomputed offline.
- LLM calls peak at about 30 at once (10 cases × 3 threads). Pick a provider and model with that headroom; the template writer covers rate-limit errors.
- If a wave holds more than 10 cases, start them in descending order of expected € at stake (need × horizon × price) and start the rest as sessions free up.

**Case coordinator loop** (one per case):

1. Open the session; load the dossiers of all suppliers in the case; compute C\_open, C\_alt, a target C and a walk-away C.
2. Start one thread negotiator per supplier, all in parallel.
3. Keep a blackboard: each supplier's standing sheet and its C, status, rival offers citable as `offer:` IDs, time left.
4. Close when any rule in the closing policy fires, or at the forced close; accepting one thread ends an RFQ.

## Policies

Policies are layered: hard guardrails always win, then the category goal sets what C rewards, the case type sets the playbook, and the supplier archetype picks the lever and tone.

### 1. Hard guardrails (code, never overridden)

- **Must-haves:** checked on every outgoing sheet and every accept, on the closing terms (sheet + supplier standard terms + fixed terms).
- **Coverage:** default `volume_per_year` = need and `contract_months` = 12 × horizon; deviate only when C says it is cheaper.
- **Accept gate:** accept only if C\_deal < C\_alt (when an alternative exists). Re-read the latest quote PDF's standard terms and `missing_fields` and recompute C first.
- **Claims:** at most 3 per message, each ID once per case, figure and ID in the same sentence, taken only from the verified claim bank.
- **Leak filter:** reject outgoing bodies that mention urgency, deadlines, budget, "no alternative", "only supplier", or any internal target or reservation figure.
- **Honesty:** never invent a rival quote or a figure; a `contradicted` claim costs trust and shows in the replay the jury reads.

### 2. Category goal

| Goal | What C rewards | Stance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `leverage` | Price, payment days, freight | Hard anchor, cite rivals and should-cost, use all rounds |
| `routine` | Little at stake | Close fast in 2-3 rounds; a fair deal beats a long fight |
| `stabilise` | Price, minus a penalty for leaving the supplier below its sustainable margin | Estimate its full cost; trade security (contract length, volume, index clause) instead of squeezing price |
| `secure_supply` | Coverage, lead time, plus the margin penalty | Cover the full need, protect lead time, no threats, never risk a walk |
| `quality_first` | `ppm_commitment` and chargebacks (high `cost_per_defect`) | Trade price for a lower ppm and a higher chargeback; ask for an 8D |

### 3. Case-type playbooks

| Type | First move | Main levers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `price_increase` | Check notice: letter `doc` days vs. contract `ctr` days. Compute the justified increase as Σ(driver weight × index change) | Latest `effective_date`, increase capped at the justified %, payment days |
| `renewal` | Compare fixed price vs. index clause via `index_paths` (a falling index makes a clause pay) | Contract length, volume, clause design (series, material share, deadband) |
| `rfq` | Same request to all bidders in parallel; then cite the best rival quote to the others | Keep at least 2 threads alive until close; accept the lowest C |
| `bundling` | Offer the combined volume across parts | Price per part for volume; all parts covered |
| `raw_material` | Model fixed vs. indexed C under the case's index path | Index clause, material share, deadband |

# Tacto Negotiation Arena - API v1

The arena speaks JSON over HTTPS. Base URL: `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1`. Every call except `/v1/data`, `/health` and
the leaderboards needs your team's key in the header `X-API-Key`. The starter kit wraps all of this in
`arena_kit.ArenaClient`. To try the API on your laptop, run `arena-sim` from the starter kit: the
same API with one plain scripted supplier - it teaches the contract, not the suppliers.

**Safe retries:** send a fresh `X-Move-Id` header (any unique string) with every `POST`. If the
network drops, repeat the request with the same `X-Move-Id`: the arena returns the answer it
already gave instead of acting twice. Reusing an id for a different request is a `422`. A request
body may be at most 64 KB.

Contents: [Flow](#flow) · [Endpoints](#endpoints) · [Messages](#messages) ·
[What counts](#what-counts) · [Documents](#documents) · [Terms](#terms) ·
[Case file](#case-file) · [Data IDs](#data-ids) ·
[Result](#result-trace-and-back-office) · [Cost and score](#cost-and-score) ·
[Live Final](#live-final-in-waves) · [Time, errors, limits](#time-errors-and-limits)

## Flow

```
GET  /v1/data                                        the data downloads (no key)
GET  /v1/me                                          your team: practice quota, best scores
GET  /v1/cases?set=practice                          the case files you can play
POST /v1/sessions                                    open a case → every supplier's quote e-mail
POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/threads/{supplier}/messages  your e-mail → the supplier's reply  (repeat)
GET  /v1/sessions/{sid}/attachments/{attachment_id}  a document the supplier attached
POST …/messages with "action": accept | walk_away    close the case → result
GET  /v1/sessions/{sid}                              state; after the end score and trace
```

## Endpoints

### Your key

One key per team - a licence. Get it on the page `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`: enter your team name and a
contact e-mail, show the match code the page displays at the Tacto desk, and once an organiser
approves, the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page
(or its link) shows the key; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it (the old key stops at once).

Send the key as `X-API-Key` with every call. A missing or unknown key is a `401`; a paused or
revoked key gets `403 "this key is paused - ask the organisers"` (or `revoked`) on every call.
There is no self-registration: `POST /v1/register` answers `403 "licences are issued by the
organisers"` (`arena-sim` keeps its own, for the simulator only).

### `GET /v1/me`

Where your team stands:

```json
{"team_name": "Haggle Hounds", "status": "active",
 "practice": {"used": 37, "left": 163, "limit": 200, "resets_at": "2026-10-11T09:42:10+00:00"},
 "best": {"case:P01": 0.71, "case:P04": 0.55}}
```
`practice`: sessions used and left in the rolling 24 hours, and when the oldest of them ages out
(the next one frees up); `best`: your best score per hosted practice case.

### `GET /v1/cases?set=practice|sandbox|final`

A list of full [case files](#case-file), so you can prepare before you open a session.

| Set | Cases | Replay |
|---|---|---|
| `practice` | all practice case files, to study; the **10 hosted** ones carry `"hosted": true` and can be played any time within your quota (a session on another is `403 "case:P06 is not hosted for practice"`); your best score per hosted case counts | right after the case |
| `sandbox` | `case:D01` (a price increase) and `case:D02` (an RFQ with two suppliers): three demo suppliers to try things on; no leaderboard | right after the case |
| `final` | the hidden cases (`"set": "hidden"`), wave by wave - see [Live Final](#live-final-in-waves); `403` before the first wave | after the final |

The replay is the same team view in every set: the e-mails as sent, terms, statuses, claim
results, the supplier's reasons in words and the score - as a real supplier would tell you. No rule
names, no internal parameters, none of the supplier's hidden figures (shown as `…`).

### `POST /v1/sessions`

`{"case_id": "case:P01"}` opens a case. Every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once (round 0);
from now on the 60-second clock runs per thread.

| Response field | |
|---|---|
| `session_id` | use in all further calls |
| `case` | the case file |
| `threads` | `{supplier_id: [opening message]}` - each supplier's quote e-mail, quote PDF attached |
| `opening` | the same quotes in the structured form of the `/moves` path |

Practice: your best score per case counts; at most 10 sessions open at a time (`429`).
**Quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** Every practice session start
answers with the header `X-Practice-Remaining: <sessions left>`. At the limit: `429` with a detail
starting `practice limit:` that names `resets_at`, `X-Practice-Remaining: 0` and no `Retry-After` -
retrying does not help before then. Sandbox and final sessions do not count. Final: one session per team and case; a second is a `409` naming the running session -
pick it up again with `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` and `GET …/threads/{supplier_id}`.

### `POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/threads/{supplier_id}/messages`

Body `{"message": Message}` (see [Messages](#messages)). Returns the supplier's reply, a Message.
With an `action`, it closes the case and returns the [result](#result-trace-and-back-office):
`{"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:…"}` takes that supplier's standing term sheet;
`{"type": "walk_away"}` ends the case without a deal.

A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**; its time never counts against your 60
seconds. Use an HTTP timeout of at least 180 s (the kit uses 180).

`422`: invalid message - nothing happens, no round is used (e.g. a term sheet without every
negotiable field, a value outside the allowed options, an unknown or stale `term_sheet_id`, more
than 3 term sheets). `409`: the thread or session has ended (in the final also at the wave's cap),
you reached the round limit (you may still accept), or your message came too late - it counted
as a timeout; `GET` the thread for the supplier's answer.

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}/threads/{supplier_id}`

The thread: `supplier_id`, `offer_id` (its standing term sheet), `status`, `closed` (why the thread
ended, else null), `messages` (all e-mails, both directions, in order; yours carry `"from":
"buyer"`), `timeouts` (the supplier's answers to your late moves). Enough to pick a case up again
after a crash.

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}/attachments/{attachment_id}`

The file of a supplier attachment (`application/pdf`, xlsx, ...), rendered from the supplier's
data. See [Documents](#documents).

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}`

The session state: `session_id`, `case_id`, `set`, `status` (`open` | `ended`), `end_reason`
(`accepted`, `walked_away`, `no_deal`, `timeout`, `wave_cap`, `window_closed`), `rounds`, `opening`, `threads`
(per supplier: `offer_id`, `status`, `offers`, `closed`, `seconds_left`) and, after the end,
`result` and `replay_url`.

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}/backoffice`

The supplier's roles talking internally (who asked whom, approvals, documents attached), in the
same team view: their words, without hidden figures or internal names. Only after the case has
ended - in the final after the final; before that `403`.

### Lists and boards

- `GET /health` - is the arena up? No key needed.
- `GET /v1/data` - the data downloads, no key needed: `{"package": {"url": "/v1/data/package.zip"},
  "release-sunday": {"public": false, "at": "2026-10-11T06:00:00+00:00"}}`. Once the Sunday
  release is public it carries `"url": "/v1/data/release-sunday.zip"` - new news, letters and a
  memo, with their own `facts.json` (new IDs only; package v1 stays as it is). Hidden cases may
  cite them; practice cases stay on package v1.

- `GET /v1/sessions?set=practice|sandbox|final` - your sessions: `session_id`, `case_id`, `status`,
  `end_reason`, `deal`, `score`, `rounds`, `created_at`.
- `GET /v1/leaderboard?set=practice|final` (JSON), `GET /leaderboard` (HTML screen) - no key
  needed. Practice: `total` = the mean of your best score per hosted case × 100 (cases not played
  count 0). Final: hidden cases only, live, as **points so far**:
  ```json
  {"set": "final", "cases": 6,
   "teams": [{"team_name": "Haggle Hounds", "played": 6, "deals": 6, "rounds": 21,
              "waves": {"1": 37.0, "2": 40.8}, "total": 77.8, "rank": 1,
              "saved_eur": 48210, "saved_eur_waves": {"1": 30115, "2": 18095}}],
   "waves": [{"n": 1, "theme": "Opening", "running": false, "closed": true, "seconds_left": 0}, …]}
  ```
  Per team, `waves` holds each started wave's score: the mean of its case scores × 100, 0-100, one
  decimal (a case you did not play scores your alternative once its wave has closed). `total` is
  the sum of those wave columns as shown - your points so far, up to 500 after five waves. Ranked by
  `total`; an exact tie goes to more `deals`, then fewer `rounds`. `cases` counts the cases of the
  waves started so far. **€ saved** (`saved_eur`, whole euros, per started wave in `saved_eur_waves`)
  is a side number and does not rank: per ended session `C_open − C_end`, where `C_end` is `c_deal`,
  or `c_alt` without a deal (0 if the case has no alternative) - money saved against the cheapest
  opening offer, over the case's horizon (`horizon_years`, 1-2 years), the same C as
  the score. It can be negative (a deal or an alternative dearer than the opening offer); a case
  you did not play saves nothing, nor does a deal that breaks a must-have (it scores 0). In the final the feed's `deal` and `no_deal` events carry it too.
  During the Live Final your agent must not read the leaderboard, the results, the screen or the
  event feed (`/v1/events`, `/v1/events/stream`, `/screen`, `/v1/screen`, `/v1/results`, `/results`)
  - they are for people.
- `GET /v1/results` (JSON), `GET /results` (page) - no key needed: the final's standings for people,
  every team: the final leaderboard above plus `"replays": true` once the final is closed. Before
  the first wave: no teams, nothing about the plan. `GET /v1/results/{team_name}` - one team's cases
  of the **started** waves: per wave `n`, `theme`, `running`, `closed`, `points`, `saved_eur` and
  `cases` - `case_id`, `title`, `type`, `suppliers` (names), `status` (`not started`, `in play`,
  `deal`, `no deal`; `not played` once its wave has closed - it scores your alternative), `end_reason`,
  `score`, `saved_eur`, `rounds`, and after the final `replay_url`. Both cached for 5 seconds.
- `GET /live` - the build page, no key needed (Sat 10:00 - Sun 12:00): every team's quota use,
  practice records and highlights.
- `GET /replay/{sid}` (link in the session's `replay_url`): a finished negotiation step by step -
  every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move in words, the same view in every set.
  Play, read the replay, improve, play again: that is the learning loop. Final: after the final,
  for everyone - the results page links each final session's replay then.

### The structured path

For agents that skip prose: `POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/moves` with `{"supplier_id": …, "move":
{"type": "offer", "offer_id": "<standing offer>", "terms": {…}, "claims": [{"type", "refs",
"asserted"}], "text": "≤ 800 chars"}}` returns a structured supplier move; `POST …/accept
{"offer_id"}` and `POST …/walk_away` close. Same supplier, same rules; claims are typed explicitly
(see [What counts](#what-counts)) instead of read from the message.

## Messages

| Field | Buyer | Supplier |
|---|---|---|
| `subject` | ≤ 300 chars | `Re: …` |
| `body` | plain text, ≤ 8,000 chars | the role in charge writes; other roles add paragraphs |
| `term_sheets` | 0-3 alternative packages `{"terms": {…}}`, each with every negotiable field | its standing offer: `{"term_sheet_id": "offer:…", "terms": {…}}` |
| `refs` | data IDs your message relies on (≤ 20); IDs written in the body count too | - |
| `attachments` | ≤ 5 × `{"name", "type": "md" \| "csv" \| "json" \| "pdf" \| "xlsx", "content_b64"}`; md, csv and json are read | `{"attachment_id", "name", "type"}` - fetch the file by id |
| `action` | `null`, `{"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id"}` or `{"type": "walk_away"}` | - |
| `from` | `buyer` | `<role>@<supplier>` |
| `status` | - | `open`, `final_offer` (its last word: push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms - you still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid` |
| `signals` | - | `reply_delay_days` (how long a real reply would have taken), `validity_days` |
| `missing_fields` | - | fields its term sheet leaves out: at a deal they close on its **standard terms** |
| `claim_results` | - | per argument the arena read from your last message: `{"index", "result"}` |
| `thread_id`, `message_id`, `in_reply_to` | optional | set |

A message without a term sheet is fine - a question, say. It is answered, and the quote stands.

A real exchange from practice case `case:P01` (Brandlhuber announces +9.5 % on volute casings,
"due to energy and wages"); the starter kit's README shows how the index figure was found:

```json
{"message": {
  "subject": "HN volute casings - your letter of 11 September",
  "body": "Dear Sir or Madam,\nthank you for your letter. We cannot follow +9.5 % from November.\nElectricity producer prices changed -3.7% from 2025-08 to 2026-08 (idx:PPI-D351@2025-08, idx:PPI-D351@2026-08).\nCould you send us a cost breakdown?\nBest regards\nHollerau Pumpenwerke, Purchasing",
  "term_sheets": [
    {"terms": {"unit_price": 129.90, "effective_date": "2027-04-01", "payment_days": 60}},
    {"terms": {"unit_price": 128.50, "effective_date": "2027-04-01", "payment_days": 14}}]}}
```
→
```json
{"thread_id": "thread:P01:70110", "message_id": "msg:70110-1-2", "from": "sales@70110",
 "subject": "Re: HN volute casings - your letter of 11 September",
 "body": "Guten Tag,\nYour requested terms change our costs; our Angebot for them follows.\nPreis €139.80 per unit, Zahlungsziel 14 Tage netto, valid from 2027-04-01.\nWe checked the index change data you cited; it holds and we took it into account.\nWe did not know that - a fair point.\nLCI-C rose 2.7 % in twelve months and is 30 % of our cost. That remains.\nPPI-C241 rose 6.5 % in twelve months and is 24 % of our cost. That remains.\nFaster payment helps our cash flow; that is reflected in the price.\nOur costs move with LCI-C, PPI-C241, PPI-D351; the figures stay with us.\nViele Grüße aus der Gießerei\nGießerei Brandlhuber GmbH & Co. KG",
 "status": "open",
 "term_sheets": [{"term_sheet_id": "offer:70110-1",
                  "terms": {"unit_price": 139.80, "payment_days": 14, "effective_date": "2027-04-01"}}],
 "missing_fields": [], "claim_results": [{"index": 0, "result": "verified"}],
 "signals": {"reply_delay_days": 2, "validity_days": 30}, "attachments": []}
```
The supplier answered the 14-day sheet at its own price for an April start, accepted the index
figure - and answered with the cost drivers that rose. (Offline wording from a local run; on the
hosted arena the supplier writes its own e-mail and may well decide differently.)

## What counts

**Term sheets bind** - nothing else. They are taken exactly as you send them, never guessed from
prose; the deal is the term sheet you accept.

**Data you cite is checked.** Cite the data by ID (in the body or in `refs`) and write your figure
in the same sentence; the arena checks it against the data package (`facts.json`) and reports each
check in the reply's `claim_results` - at most 3 per message, so write one argument per sentence.
Order lines of different parts are separate arguments, so citing orders for three parts uses all
three. Without a figure, the data's own value is taken. IDs of meeting notes, suppliers or parts
are context, not checks.

| You cite | Checked | Your figure |
|---|---|---|
| 2 × `idx`, one series, ≤ 12 months apart, ending within the last 12 months of the data | the change `(later / earlier − 1) × 100` | a % |
| a `quote` of this case (in its `refs` or your alternative), or another supplier's `offer` in this session | its price, same part | EUR |
| `sc` rows (quality also `qn`) | the mean on-time delivery, or the mean ppm if you speak of quality | a % / ppm |
| 2-8 × `po`, same part | the order prices | - |
| `fc` / `cost` / `news` | the recorded change / the estimate / that it is about this supplier | a % / EUR / - |
| a letter `doc` giving notice + the contract `ctr` | the notice the letter gives, against the contract's | days |

Tolerance: ±0.5 percentage points for %, else ±0.5 % (at least 0.01). Results: `verified` - the
data matches; whether and how far it moves the supplier is the supplier's business. `irrelevant` -
true, but not about this supplier or part, or an index window too long or too old.
`contradicted` - an unknown ID or a wrong figure: it costs trust. `duplicate` - each ID counts
once per case, except a rival's quote: in an RFQ you may cite it to every other bidder, and it
counts once per supplier. Citing a buyer-private fact - a rival quote - reveals it to the
supplier you cite it to.

**Verified is not the same as convincing.** A supplier's hard limits come from its own economics
and authority: its cost floor, its boss's approval for bigger moves, no concession without a move
from you. Inside them it decides as the person it is. True data may disarm it, move it a little,
or meet "that's not our reality" because something else weighs more for it right now - its notes,
letters, news and quote remarks show what. Identical messages need not get identical replies.

**What you write is understood** - questions, arguments, signals of urgency or of having no
alternative, a budget, threats, appreciation, tone, attempts to manipulate - and has consequences,
as it would with a person. Questions go to the person in charge, who answers as openly as the
company is. Cheaper engineering variants a supplier mentions are information, not binding terms.

## Documents

Rendered from the supplier's structured state - never written by a language model, byte-stable.

| Document | When | What matters |
|---|---|---|
| Quote PDF | opening e-mail; with `final_offer` and `agreed` | offered terms, **the standard terms that apply to everything not stated**, terms fixed by your enquiry, validity |
| Cost breakdown XLSX | you asked and the supplier is open enough | elements in EUR per unit and their share (formulas) |
| 8D report PDF | quality topics | scorecards, the 8D steps, a ppm commitment |
| Delivery schedule XLSX | delivery and capacity topics | monthly quantities, lead time |
| Order confirmation PDF | at the deal | the agreed terms |

## Terms

Every term with € weight is a structured field. A term sheet carries **exactly** the case's
`negotiable` fields; `fixed_terms` hold the rest. Every negotiable field except `unit_price` takes
a value from `term_options` (or the supplier's standard value).

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `unit_price` | number, € with 2 decimals, per the part's `price_unit` | price |
| `payment_days` | int, 0-120 | days net |
| `lead_time_days` | int | order to delivery |
| `volume_per_year` | int | binding annual units |
| `contract_months` | int, 0-36 | 0 = a single order (counts as one year's lot) |
| `effective_date` | ISO date | from when the new price applies |
| `index_clause` | null or `{series, material_share, deadband_pct, base_month}` | the price follows an index |
| `incoterm` | `EXW`, `FCA`, `DAP` | freight per unit from the case file |
| `tooling_eur` | € | one-off |
| `ppm_commitment` | int | committed defect rate |
| `chargeback_eur_per_complaint` | € | what the supplier pays per complaint |

## Case file

Case files come through the API, not in the data package: `GET /v1/cases?set=practice|sandbox`
any time, `GET /v1/cases?set=final` wave by wave.

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `case_id`, `set`, `type` | `type`: `price_increase`, `renewal`, `rfq`, `bundling`, `raw_material`, `capacity`, `quality` |
| `title`, `briefing` | the situation, in prose |
| `trigger_doc` | the document that started it, e.g. the supplier's letter |
| `parts`, `suppliers` | what is negotiated, with whom (2-3 suppliers = an RFQ) |
| `negotiable`, `fixed_terms`, `term_options` | see [Terms](#terms) |
| `buyer` | your need and rates, below |
| `round_limit` | your messages per thread, default 10 |
| `refs` | data the case points to - a start, not the whole story |
| `facts` | hidden cases: facts that exist only in this case (e.g. a new letter), in the format of `facts.json`, citable in this case |

`buyer`:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `need_per_year`, `horizon_years` | the need the deal should cover, and over how many years (≤ 3) |
| `current_unit_price` | what you pay until a new price takes effect |
| `fallback_unit_price` | what uncovered need costs (re-tender or spot, incl. switching) |
| `interest_rate`, `reference_payment_days` | your cost of money per year; your standard payment term |
| `need_lead_time_days`, `late_cost_per_day` | the lead time you need; € per day beyond it |
| `cost_per_defect` | € per defective part |
| `category_goal` | `stabilise` (strategic), `secure_supply` (bottleneck), `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - the company's category strategy for this part; the briefing says it in words, and the rates in this block follow it |
| `fallback_risk_pct` | % added to what uncovered need costs: buying it later is a risk |
| `index_risk_pct` | % of the indexed spend: the risk you carry with an index clause |
| `sustainable_margin_pct`, `relationship_eur_per_point` | `stabilise` and `secure_supply` only: the margin a healthy supplier needs, and € per margin point and year that a deal leaves it below |
| `freight_eur_per_unit` | `{EXW, FCA, DAP}` |
| `index_paths` | `{series: change}` - the expected index move over the horizon, `0.04` = +4% |
| `must_haves` | `[{field, op, value}]`, `op` one of `<=`, `>=`, `<`, `>`, `==`, `!=`; a deal that breaks one scores 0 |
| `alternative` | `{kind: none \| quote \| current_contract, ref, terms}` - what you get without a deal |

## Data IDs

IDs have the form `<type>:<id>[@period]`, are unique across the package and sit in the first
column of each table. `facts.json` in the package lists every citable ID with the values the arena
checks:

| ID | Fields |
|---|---|
| `idx:<series>@YYYY-MM` | `series`, `month`, `value` |
| `quote:` | `part`, `supplier`, `unit_price` (+ the quote's other terms) |
| `sc:<supplier>@YYYYQn` | `supplier`, `otd_pct`, `ppm` |
| `qn:` | `supplier`, `part`, `ppm` |
| `po:` | `supplier`, `part`, `unit_price` |
| `cost:<part>` | `part`, `unit_cost` |
| `fc:<part>@YYYY-MM` | `part`, `change_pct` |
| `news:` | `supplier` (or null) |
| `doc:` | `supplier`, `date`, `days` (notice given), `asked_price` (price letters) |
| `ctr:` | `supplier`, `days` (notice agreed) |

Offers made in the session are citable as `offer:` IDs.

## Result, trace and back office

Closing returns the result (without the trace); `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` adds the trace after the
end - in the final after the final. The numbers are exact in every set: your score, `c_open`,
`c_best` and the cost breakdown, relationship charge included.

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `ended`, `deal`, `must_haves_ok` | |
| `supplier_id`, `offer_id`, `terms` | who and what you closed - fields the term sheet left out filled with the supplier's standard terms |
| `c_open`, `c_deal`, `c_alt`, `c_best` | see [Cost and score](#cost-and-score); `c_alt` is your alternative |
| `score` | 0-1 |
| `cost_breakdown` | `c_deal` by part: price, uncovered_need, fallback_risk, payment_terms, freight, late_delivery, quality, tooling, index_clause, index_risk, relationship |
| `trace` | after the end (final: after the final), per move, in every set: `{round, actor, move, reasons}` - `move` is the e-mail as sent with its terms, status and claim results, `reasons` the supplier's reasons in words (figures it keeps to itself shown as `…`) |

## Cost and score

With `N` = `need_per_year`, `H` = `horizon_years`, `V` = `volume_per_year`, `M` =
`contract_months`, `P` = `unit_price`, `r` = `interest_rate`, `d_ref` = `reference_payment_days`:

```
years     = min(M / 12, H); a single order (M = 0) counts as 1   a commitment beyond the horizon
committed = V · years                                          neither costs nor earns
covered   = min(V, N) · years
pre       = units bought between the horizon start and effective_date (at current_unit_price)
new       = (committed − pre) · P                              bought at the new price
spend     = pre · current_unit_price + new
uncovered = (N · H − covered) · fallback_unit_price
C = spend
  + uncovered · (1 + fallback_risk_pct / 100)                  uncovered need, and its risk
  + spend · r · (d_ref − payment_days) / 360                   paying earlier costs interest
  + committed · freight_eur_per_unit[incoterm]
  + late_cost_per_day · max(0, lead_time_days − need_lead_time_days)
  + committed · ppm_commitment / 1e6 · (cost_per_defect − min(chargeback_eur_per_complaint, cost_per_defect))
  + tooling_eur
  + new · material_share · max(0, |index_path| − deadband_pct / 100) · sign(index_path)   with an index clause
  + new · material_share · index_risk_pct / 100                                            with an index clause
  + relationship_eur_per_point · soft(sustainable_margin_pct − supplier_margin_pct) · years
                                                               stabilise and secure_supply only
soft(g) = 0 for g ≤ 0;  g² / 10 for 0 < g ≤ 5;  g − 2.5 for g > 5   (margin points: gentle, no kink)
```

The horizon starts at the fixed or earliest `effective_date` option; `index_path` is the case's
expected move of the clause's series.

**The supplier's margin** is `(value − full_cost) / value × 100`: `full_cost` is the supplier's
full cost per unit, `value` what the deal is worth to it in cash per unit - the price at its own
standard terms that would pay it the same: the price (units sold before the new price applies at
the current price), payment timing and tooling paid up front at what money is worth to **it** now
(more to a supplier short of cash), the freight leg it carries, chargebacks at the defect rate it
really has, and what a faster delivery, a larger volume or a tighter defect commitment costs or
brings it. A longer contract or an index clause is security for it, not cash, and does not count.
So a cash-short supplier that trades a lower price for faster payment is not squeezed.
You don't know its cost and rates - estimate them (should-cost data, its quotes, what it tells
you). `arena_kit.total_cost(case, terms, standard, supplier)` computes C, with
`arena_kit.cost.supplier_value` for your estimate of the supplier.

```
score = clip((C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best), 0, 1)
```

`C_open`: the cheapest opening quote (among those that keep the must-haves). `C_best`: the cheaper
of your alternative and the best package any supplier in the case would accept with every valid
lever applied. No deal scores the alternative (0 if none); a broken must-have scores 0; if `C_open
− C_best` ≤ €0.01, a deal at `C_best` scores 1. Team total = mean case score × 100.

## Live Final in waves

The hidden cases come in 5 themed waves. The host introduces each wave on the big screen, then
starts it; a wave holds several cases that appear at its start, for every team at the same moment.
Before a wave starts, the API names nothing of it - not its theme, its cases or how many there are:
`GET /v1/cases?set=final` answers `403` until the first wave starts, and a session on a case of a
wave not started yet is a `404 "no such case"`, like any unknown ID. Once waves have started,
the list holds the case files of every started wave, each with four more fields:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `wave`, `theme` | the wave's number and the theme the host revealed |
| `open` | `true` while the wave runs; you can open sessions for its cases only then (after its end: `403 "<case> belongs to wave <n>, which is not running"`) |
| `seconds_left` | until the wave's cap - 8 minutes for every wave (the host may extend one); read it, don't assume it |

Inside a wave, each team gets the cases in its own order. One session per case; a second `POST
/v1/sessions` is a `409` naming the running session - pick it up with `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` and
`GET …/threads/{supplier_id}`. **At the cap every session of the wave still open ends without a
deal** (`end_reason: wave_cap`, the alternative's score); later calls get a `409`. Each wave scores
0-100 for your team; the board adds them up as your points so far. Poll the case
list every few seconds and keep your agent running until the last wave has closed - `arena run
--set final` in the starter kit does this.

## Time, errors and limits

- **60 seconds per message**, per thread, counted from the supplier's reply. A message later than
  that counts as a timeout: your last offer is repeated and the supplier's patience drops (`409`,
  the answer is in the thread). Three timeouts in a row, or one after the last round, end the
  thread.
- **A supplier's reply can take up to about a minute** - its time never counts against your 60
  seconds. Use an HTTP timeout of at least 180 s (the kit uses 180).
- **Limits per key:** 10 calls per second, 10 open sessions. A Live Final wave holds several cases
  that appear at its start and gives you 8 minutes: play them all in parallel.

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| `401` | missing or unknown `X-API-Key` |
| `403` | paused or revoked key; a practice case that is not hosted; `POST /v1/register` (keys come from `/apply`); the final's case list before the first wave; a final case whose wave has ended; back office before the end |
| `404`

# brief

- `brief.md` - the participant brief (max. 4 pages)
- `api.md` - the HTTP API reference
- `submission.md` - what to submit on Sunday, and how the pitch works
=====BRIEF=====
# Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief

> **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers,
> gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.**

## 1. The story

You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker:
centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in
Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals,
motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the
inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework
contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix
its quality.

You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a
small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must
approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their
topics and attach documents.

Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source
every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data -
orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes
from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In
Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.)

## 2. The task

Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case
file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your
**buyer agent**

1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package;
2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative
   packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like;
3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away.

**How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the
desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job
shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its
own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data
you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it
decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you
signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship
as people do; padding does not buy price.

**Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") -
or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces
are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the
supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care
more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still
move on other terms.

## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00)

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` |
| **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` |
| **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) |
| **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes |

You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT.

**Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail,
and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once**
on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it.
Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive).

**Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what
you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use,
practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00.

**`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing
right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want
a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real
suppliers act is part of the challenge.

**The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open
the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them -
improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts.

## 4. The data

The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts,
invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past
negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the
long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30).

- **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `<type>:<id>[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`,
  `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`.
- What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are
  just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional.
- **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October
  (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it.

## 5. How a negotiation works

- **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
- **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
  field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
- **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
  `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
  still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;
  and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**;
  its time never counts against your 60 seconds.
- **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3
  suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
- **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
  from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
  a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
  the last round, end the thread.
- **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF.

**Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before

contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix
its quality.

You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a
small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must
approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their
topics and attach documents.

Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source
every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data -
orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes
from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In
Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.)

Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case
file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your

   packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like;

**How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the
desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job
shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its
own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data
you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it
decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you
signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship
as people do; padding does not buy price.

or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces

supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care
